title: Medical Spanish for the ED
summary: Practical Spanish for an emergency department where a large share of patients speak it: the interpreter rule first, then the pronunciation, phrases, and commands that let you room a patient, take vitals, draw blood, and offer comfort, plus the words you must recognize the second a family member says them.

lessons.title: The interpreter rule comes first
lessons.body:
## Why this is a legal question, not a preference

A patient who cannot comfortably discuss their care in English is described as having **limited English proficiency (LEP)**. Under Title VI of the Civil Rights Act and Section 1557 of the Affordable Care Act, a hospital that takes federal money must provide language assistance **free of charge** and may not ask the patient to supply their own interpreter. A patient is never billed for it and is never told to come back with someone who speaks English.

That is the floor. The reason it exists is that language errors are clinical errors. A missed allergy. A misread `once`, which in Spanish is the number eleven, not the English word once. A consent signature from someone who never understood what they agreed to.

> **Key:** Your Spanish is for rapport, comfort, and simple task commands. A qualified interpreter is for history, consent, and anything where a misunderstanding changes care.

## Where the line sits

| You can do this yourself | This needs the interpreter |
|---|---|
| `Hola, me llamo...` | Chief complaint and history |
| `Voy a tomarle la presión.` | Allergies and the medication list for the chart |
| `Respire profundo.` | Consent for any procedure |
| `¿Le duele aquí?` | Discharge instructions |
| `¿Quiere agua?` | Refusal of care or leaving against advice |
| Counting `cero` to `diez` for a pain score | Anything carrying a risk or a number that matters |

If you are not sure which column you are in, you are in the right column.

## Never a child, and rarely a family member

An ad hoc interpreter is anyone untrained: a relative, a friend, a bilingual staff member pulled out of a hallway. Studies of ad hoc interpreters find far more clinically significant errors than with trained interpreters, and the errors skew toward **omission**, the kind that make a patient sound better than they are.

Family also filters. A husband will not interpret `me pega` (he hits me). A grown son may not say the word cancer to his mother. Using a **child** as an interpreter is not acceptable in any non-emergent situation.

The one exception is a true emergency where seconds decide the outcome and no interpreter can be reached. Use whatever you have, get qualified help immediately after, and document exactly what happened.

## The workflow, step by step

1. Ask and record the **preferred language for medical care**, not just that someone speaks Spanish. Some patients speak Spanish second and an indigenous language at home.
2. Get the device: the dual-handset phone, the video cart (video remote interpreting, or VRI), or the in-person interpreter if your hospital staffs one.
3. Dial the vendor, give the account number and the language, and note the interpreter ID they read out.
4. Introduce the room by role, not by name: an ED tech, a patient, a family member at the bedside.
5. **Speak to the patient.** Say "When did the pain start?" and look at the patient. Do not say "Ask her when the pain started."
6. One idea per sentence, then stop. Long paragraphs get summarized, and summary is where the error lives.
7. No side conversations in English in the room.
8. **Document** it: interpreter used, modality, and the interpreter ID number.

> **On shift:** Find the interpreter phone and the video cart on your first shift, before you need them, and learn the account number. Two minutes of scavenger hunting in a room with a frightened patient is two minutes you do not have.

## Four phrases for the gap

| Spanish | Say it | Meaning | When to use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `¿Prefiere hablar en español?` | pray-FYEH-reh ah-BLAR en es-pah-NYOL | Do you prefer to speak Spanish? | Confirming the language |
| `Voy a llamar a un intérprete.` | boy ah yah-MAR ah oon een-TEHR-preh-teh | I am going to call an interpreter. | Immediately after |
| `Ya viene el intérprete.` | yah BYEH-neh el een-TEHR-preh-teh | The interpreter is coming. | While you dial |
| `Un momento, por favor.` | oon mo-MEN-toh por fah-BOR | One moment, please. | Any pause |
keyPoints: Interpreter services are free to the patient and required by federal law; the patient never has to bring their own.
Use your own Spanish for greetings, comfort, and task commands only. History, consent, and discharge go through an interpreter.
Never use a child as an interpreter, and use a family member only in a true emergency with no alternative.
Speak to the patient, not to the interpreter, one idea per sentence.
Document interpreter use: modality and interpreter ID number.

checks.q: A Spanish-speaking patient's adult son offers to interpret so you can get the medication list charted faster. What do you do?
choices: Let him interpret; he is family and it saves the department time
Use the son for the medication list but call an interpreter for consent
Thank him, tell the patient the interpreter is coming, and get the medication list through the qualified interpreter
Ask the patient to write the list out in English
checks.why: The medication list goes in the chart and drives dosing and interaction decisions, so it is clinical content and needs a qualified interpreter. Family members omit and filter. Writing it in English asks the patient to solve the hospital's legal obligation.

checks.q: Which of these can you say to a Spanish-speaking patient without an interpreter on the line?
choices: That the doctor is considering surgery
`Voy a tomarle la presión` (I am going to take your blood pressure)
That they need to sign the CT consent form
That a test result came back abnormal
checks.why: A blood pressure cuff is a simple, low-risk task command with no decision attached. Surgery, consent, and results are clinical conversations with consequences, and all three require a qualified interpreter.

checks.q: The interpreter picks up. How should you phrase your first question?
choices: "Tell her we need to know about her pain."
"When did the pain start?" said to the patient while looking at her
"Can you find out her pain history for me?"
checks.why: You speak directly to the patient in the first person and let the interpreter relay it. Framing everything as ask her or tell her turns the patient into a third party in her own encounter and invites the interpreter to summarize.

lessons.title: Sounding right in ten minutes
lessons.body:
## Five vowels that never change

English vowels are chaos: the letter a in cat, car, care, and cake is four different sounds. Spanish has exactly five vowel sounds and they are the same every single time.

| Letter | Sound | Like the English | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `a` | ah | father | `cama` (KAH-mah), bed |
| `e` | eh | bet | `pecho` (PEH-choh), chest |
| `i` | ee | see | `sí` (see), yes |
| `o` | oh | boat, but short and flat | `ojo` (OH-hoh), eye |
| `u` | oo | food | `mucho` (MOO-choh), a lot |

If you get nothing else right, get the vowels right and you will be understood. Keep them short, flat, and pure. Do not glide them the way English does.

## The consonants that trip people

- `j` is an English h made a little further back in the throat. `ojo` is OH-hoh, `hija` (daughter) is EE-hah.
- `g` before e or i is that same h sound: `alergia` is ah-LEHR-hyah. Before a, o, or u it is a hard g: `gota` is GOH-tah.
- `h` is always silent. `hospital` is os-pee-TAHL, `herida` (wound) is eh-REE-dah.
- `ll` is a y. `me llamo` is meh YAH-moh, `pastillas` is pas-TEE-yahs.
- `ñ` is ny, the sound in canyon. `año` (year) is AH-nyoh, `mañana` is mah-NYAH-nah.
- `rr` and a word-initial `r` are trilled. A perfect trill is not required; a light tap of the tongue is enough and nobody will mishear you.
- `qu` is a plain k. `¿qué?` is keh.
- `v` and `b` are the same soft sound. `voy` comes out closer to boy.
- `z`, and `c` before e or i, are an s across Latin America. `cero` is SEH-roh, `corazón` is koh-rah-SOHN.

> **Trap:** `ll` and `j` are the two that break whole sentences. If you say meh LAH-moh and ah-ler-JEE-ah, people squint. Say meh YAH-moh and ah-LEHR-hyah.

## Where the stress goes

Three rules cover nearly every word you will meet.

1. The word ends in a **vowel, n, or s**: stress the **second-to-last** syllable. `pecho` is PEH-choh, `duele` is DWEH-leh.
2. The word ends in any other consonant: stress the **last** syllable. `dolor` is doh-LOR, `hospital` is os-pee-TAHL.
3. There is a written accent mark: stress **exactly there**, no exceptions. `corazón` is koh-rah-SOHN, `médico` is MEH-dee-koh, `presión` is preh-SYON.

Stress carries meaning, and sometimes clinical meaning. `tomo` is I take. `tomó` is he or she took. In a history that is the difference between a home medication and a one-time overdose.

## The upside-down punctuation

`¿` and `¡` open a question or an exclamation. They are a reading aid, not decoration: they tell you a sentence is a question before you start reading it out loud, so your voice rises in the right place.

> **On shift:** Nobody expects an accent. Patients hear effort, not polish. Slow and clear beats fast and mumbled, and slow is also what a frightened person needs.

## Say these five out loud

These five sentences contain every sound above. Drill them until they come out without thinking.

- `Hola, me llamo...` is OH-lah, meh YAH-moh
- `¿Le duele aquí?` is leh DWEH-leh ah-KEE
- `Voy a sacarle sangre.` is boy ah sah-KAR-leh SAHN-greh
- `Respire profundo.` is res-PEE-reh proh-FOON-doh
- `¿Tiene alergias?` is TYEH-neh ah-LEHR-hyahs
keyPoints: Five vowels, one sound each, always: ah, eh, ee, oh, oo.
`j` and `g` before e or i are an English h; `h` is silent; `ll` is y; `ñ` is ny.
Ends in a vowel, n, or s: stress the second-to-last syllable. Ends in another consonant: stress the last. A written accent overrides both.
`tomo` versus `tomó` is I take versus he took; stress can change a medication history.
Slow and clear is better than fast and accented.

checks.q: How is `alergia` pronounced?
checks.why: The g before an i is the throaty h sound, and the word ends in a vowel so the stress falls on the second-to-last syllable. A hard English g or a j sound is the single most common mispronunciation of this word.

checks.q: Which word is stressed on its last syllable?
checks.why: `dolor` ends in r, a consonant other than n or s, so the stress goes to the last syllable: doh-LOR. `pecho`, `duele`, and `cama` all end in vowels, so each is stressed on the second-to-last syllable.

checks.q: A patient says `tomó` with the stress on the second syllable. What does that tell you?
choices: It is present tense: I take it
It is past tense: he or she took it
It is a command: take it
Stress does not change the meaning
checks.why: The written accent on the final o marks a past-tense third person. `tomo` (TOH-moh) is I take, an ongoing home medication. `tomó` (toh-MOH) is he or she took, which in an overdose history is an entirely different problem.

lessons.title: Hello, my name is, and may I
lessons.body:
## The first fifteen seconds

The way you enter a room sets everything after it. In Spanish-speaking cultures a greeting is not optional politeness the way an American nod is; walking in and going straight to the arm with a blood pressure cuff reads as rude, even when the patient never says so.

Greet, name yourself, say your role, then ask before you touch. That is a fifteen-second routine and it buys you the rest of the encounter.

| Spanish | Say it | Meaning | When to use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Buenos días.` | BWEH-nohs DEE-ahs | Good morning. | Until about noon |
| `Buenas tardes.` | BWEH-nahs TAR-dehs | Good afternoon. | Noon to dark |
| `Buenas noches.` | BWEH-nahs NOH-chehs | Good evening. | After dark, and on nights |
| `Hola, me llamo Jose.` | OH-lah, meh YAH-moh | Hello, my name is Jose. | Every introduction |
| `Soy técnico de emergencias.` | soy TEK-nee-koh deh eh-mer-HEN-syahs | I am an emergency technician. | Naming your role |
| `Soy técnica de emergencias.` | soy TEK-nee-kah | Same, said by a woman | The ending agrees with the speaker |
| `No hablo mucho español.` | noh AH-bloh MOO-choh es-pah-NYOL | I do not speak much Spanish. | Honest, and it lowers expectations |

## Usted, not tú

Spanish has two words for you. `tú` (too) is familiar, for children, close friends, and family. `usted` (oos-TED) is formal and respectful. **In a hospital you use `usted` with every adult, every time**, and you keep using it even after the patient warms up to you.

The practical effect is the verb ending. `¿Cómo se siente?` (usted) rather than `¿Cómo te sientes?` (tú). Every phrase in this module is already in the usted form, so you do not have to think about it.

Use titles the same way: `señor` (seh-NYOR) for a man, `señora` (seh-NYOH-rah) for an adult woman, `señorita` for a young woman. `Don` and `Doña` plus a first name are a warm, high-respect form common with older Caribbean and Mexican patients: Don Ramón, Doña Carmen.

> **Trap:** Using `tú` with an older adult sounds like talking down to a child. It is the single easiest way to lose an elder patient's trust in one sentence.

## Asking permission before touching

Every hands-on task gets a two-part script: say what you are about to do, then ask. `Voy a...` means I am going to. `¿Puedo...?` means may I.

| Spanish | Say it | Meaning | When to use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Con permiso.` | kon per-MEE-soh | Excuse me / with your permission. | Entering, reaching across, moving a blanket |
| `¿Puedo examinarle el brazo?` | PWEH-doh ek-sah-mee-NAR-leh el BRAH-soh | May I look at your arm? | Before uncovering anything |
| `Voy a levantarle la manga.` | boy ah leh-bahn-TAR-leh lah MAHN-gah | I am going to roll up your sleeve. | Blood pressure, IV site |
| `¿Está bien?` | es-TAH byen | Is that okay? | After any `Voy a...` |
| `Dígame si le duele.` | DEE-gah-meh see leh DWEH-leh | Tell me if it hurts. | Any painful task |
| `Perdón.` / `Lo siento.` | per-DOHN / loh SYEN-toh | Sorry. / I am sorry. | After causing pain, or for a wait |
| `Gracias.` / `Por favor.` | GRAH-syahs / por fah-BOR | Thank you. / Please. | Constantly |

## The two identifiers

You still have to confirm identity before a specimen, a wristband, or a blood draw, and that is a task you can do yourself.

- `¿Me dice su nombre completo?` (meh DEE-seh soo NOM-breh kom-PLEH-toh) is Can you tell me your full name?
- `¿Su fecha de nacimiento?` (soo FEH-chah deh nah-see-MYEN-toh) is Your date of birth?

Ask open, never leading. Do not say `¿Es usted María García?`, because a frightened or hard-of-hearing patient will say yes to almost anything.

> **On shift:** Spanish names normally carry two surnames: father's first, mother's second, as in María Elena García Rivera. Registration systems mangle this constantly, so expect the wristband and the verbal answer to differ in order. Confirm with the date of birth before you decide it is the wrong patient.
keyPoints: Greet, name yourself, state your role, then ask before touching. Fifteen seconds buys the whole encounter.
Use `usted` with every adult patient, always; `tú` with an adult sounds condescending.
`Voy a...` announces what you are about to do; `¿Puedo...?` asks permission; `Con permiso` covers entering and reaching.
Identify with two open questions: full name and date of birth, never a leading yes-or-no.
Spanish names carry two surnames, so wristband order often differs from what the patient says.

checks.q: You are a woman introducing yourself as an emergency technician. Which is correct?
checks.why: The ending agrees with the speaker, so a woman says `técnica`. `Estoy` is the temporary form of to be and is wrong for a profession, which takes `soy`.

checks.q: An 80-year-old man is your patient. Which form of address is right?
choices: His first name only, the way American staff often do
Either one; the distinction is not used in medicine
checks.why: `usted` plus a title is the respectful default for every adult, and it matters most with elders. `tú` reads as talking to a child, and jumping straight to a first name skips a courtesy most older patients expect.

checks.q: You need to verify identity before drawing blood. The best question is:
choices: Check the wristband only and say nothing
checks.why: An open question makes the patient produce the name. Any leading yes-or-no invites a reflex yes from someone anxious, hard of hearing, or trying to be agreeable, which is exactly how wrong-patient errors happen.

lessons.title: Numbers, age, weight, and the zero to ten
lessons.body:
## Why numbers come before grammar

Almost everything a tech collects is a number: an age, a weight, a pain score, a blood pressure, a room. Numbers are also the easiest part of a language, because there are only about thirty words and then they combine.

| Number | Spanish | Say it |
|---|---|---|
| 0-5 | `cero, uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco` | SEH-roh, OO-noh, dohs, trehs, KWAH-troh, SEEN-koh |
| 6-10 | `seis, siete, ocho, nueve, diez` | says, SYEH-teh, OH-choh, NWEH-beh, dyess |
| 11-15 | `once, doce, trece, catorce, quince` | OHN-seh, DOH-seh, TREH-seh, kah-TOR-seh, KEEN-seh |
| 16-19 | `dieciséis, diecisiete, dieciocho, diecinueve` | dyeh-see-SAYS and so on |
| 20-29 | `veinte, veintiuno, veintidós...` | BAYN-teh, bayn-tee-OO-noh |
| tens | `treinta, cuarenta, cincuenta, sesenta, setenta, ochenta, noventa, cien` | TRAYN-tah, kwah-REN-tah, seen-KWEN-tah, seh-SEN-tah, seh-TEN-tah, oh-CHEN-tah, noh-BEN-tah, syen |

Above thirty you join with `y` (ee), meaning and: `treinta y dos` is thirty-two, `sesenta y ocho` is sixty-eight. That is the whole system to one hundred.

> **Trap:** `once` is eleven, not the English word once. A patient who answers `once` to a question about pills took eleven of them. This false friend has caused real overdoses to be missed.

## Age and weight

| Spanish | Say it | Meaning | When to use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `¿Cuántos años tiene?` | KWAN-tohs AH-nyohs TYEH-neh | How old are you? | Registration, pediatric dosing |
| `¿Cuántos meses tiene?` | KWAN-tohs MEH-sehs | How many months old? | Infants |
| `¿Cuánto pesa?` | KWAN-toh PEH-sah | How much do you weigh? | Any weight-based dose |
| `¿En libras o en kilos?` | en LEE-brahs oh en KEE-lohs | In pounds or kilos? | Clarifying the unit |
| `Voy a pesarlo.` / `Voy a pesarla.` | boy ah peh-SAR-loh / -lah | I am going to weigh you. | At the scale |

Units matter more than the Spanish does. Patients from Latin America usually answer in **kilos**; patients raised in the United States answer in **pounds**. A 70 that is actually kilos charted as pounds is a 100-pound dosing error. Always ask `¿en libras o en kilos?` and chart the unit you were told.

## The pain score

| Spanish | Say it | Meaning | When to use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `¿Del cero al diez, cuánto le duele?` | del SEH-roh al dyess, KWAN-toh leh DWEH-leh | From zero to ten, how much does it hurt? | Every pain reassessment |
| `Cero es nada, diez es lo peor.` | SEH-roh es NAH-dah, dyess es loh peh-OR | Zero is nothing, ten is the worst. | Anchoring the scale |
| `¿Está mejor o peor?` | es-TAH meh-HOR oh peh-OR | Better or worse? | After medication |
| `¿Igual?` | ee-GWAL | The same? | Same purpose |

Hold up ten fingers while you say it. The gesture does most of the work, and it lets a patient who cannot hear well or is short of breath answer by pointing.

## Reading numbers back

You also need to **say** numbers: a room, a blood pressure, a time. Blood pressure is read as two numbers: `ciento veinte sobre ochenta` (`sobre` means over). Temperature is almost always Celsius outside the United States, so a patient who says `tengo treinta y ocho` means a fever of `38 C`, which is `100.4 F`.

> **On shift:** When a patient rattles off a number too fast, hold up fingers and count aloud. Ten fingers and a slow `uno, dos, tres` gets you a clean answer with no grammar involved.
keyPoints: Numbers to 100: learn 0 to 15, the teens pattern, the tens, and join with `y`.
`once` means eleven, not the English once. Never let that slide in a pill-count history.
Always ask `¿en libras o en kilos?` and chart the unit; kilos charted as pounds is a large dosing error.
`¿Del cero al diez, cuánto le duele?` with ten fingers held up gets a pain score from almost anyone.
A patient saying `treinta y ocho` for temperature means 38 C, which is 100.4 F.

checks.q: You ask how many pills a patient took and she answers `once`. What do you chart and escalate?
checks.why: `once` (OHN-seh) is the Spanish number eleven. Hearing it as the English word once turns an eleven-pill ingestion into a single dose, which is one of the classic false-friend errors in an emergency department.

checks.q: A patient answers `setenta` when you ask her weight. What must you do next?
choices: Ask `¿en libras o en kilos?` and chart the unit she gives
checks.why: Seventy kilos is about 154 pounds, so guessing wrong is a roughly 84-pound error on every weight-based dose. The number alone is meaningless without the unit, and patients from Latin America usually mean kilos.

checks.q: Which phrase asks a patient to rate pain from zero to ten?
choices: `¿Del cero al diez, cuánto le duele?`
checks.why: `¿Del cero al diez, cuánto le duele?` asks for severity. `¿Dónde?` asks where, `¿Desde cuándo?` asks how long, and `¿Le duele aquí?` is a yes-or-no about one spot you are pressing.

lessons.title: Where it hurts and what kind of hurt
lessons.body:
## Two ways to say pain

Spanish carries pain two ways and you need both.

`el dolor` (doh-LOR) is the noun, pain. `dolor de cabeza` is headache, `dolor de pecho` is chest pain, `dolor de estómago` is stomach pain. Any body part slots in after `dolor de`.

`me duele` (meh DWEH-leh) is the verb, literally it hurts me. The patient says `me duele el pecho`. You say `¿le duele el pecho?`, which is does your chest hurt. Plural things take `duelen`: `me duelen las piernas`, my legs hurt.

> **Key:** Learn `dolor de` plus a body part and `¿le duele aquí?` (leh DWEH-leh ah-KEE, does it hurt here). Those two carry an entire pain assessment when you pair them with pointing.

## The body, head down

| Spanish | Say it | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `la cabeza` | lah kah-BEH-sah | head |
| `el ojo` / `el oído` / `la oreja` | el OH-hoh / el oh-EE-doh / lah oh-REH-hah | eye / inner ear / outer ear |
| `la garganta` | lah gar-GAHN-tah | throat |
| `el cuello` | el KWEH-yoh | neck |
| `el pecho` | el PEH-choh | chest |
| `la espalda` | lah es-PAHL-dah | back |
| `el estómago` / `la barriga` | el es-TOH-mah-goh / lah bah-REE-gah | stomach / belly |
| `el costado` | el kos-TAH-doh | side, flank |
| `el brazo` / `el codo` / `la muñeca` / `la mano` | el BRAH-soh / el KOH-doh / lah moo-NYEH-kah / lah MAH-noh | arm / elbow / wrist / hand |
| `la cadera` / `la pierna` / `la rodilla` | lah kah-DEH-rah / lah PYER-nah / lah roh-DEE-yah | hip / leg / knee |
| `el tobillo` / `el pie` | el toh-BEE-yoh / el pyeh | ankle / foot |
| `el corazón` / `los pulmones` | el koh-rah-SOHN / lohs pool-MOH-nehs | heart / lungs |

`la barriga` and `la panza` are the everyday words for belly and are what you will actually hear. `el vientre` is the formal one you will see in writing.

## The quality of the pain

This vocabulary is what you listen for, not what you say. When a patient volunteers one of these, it goes in the nurse's ear.

| Spanish | Say it | Meaning | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|---|
| `presión` / `opresión` | preh-SYON / oh-preh-SYON | pressure / tightness | Classic cardiac description |
| `ardor` / `me arde` | ar-DOR / meh AR-deh | burning | Reflux, urinary, or cardiac |
| `punzante` | poon-SAHN-teh | stabbing | Pleuritic, musculoskeletal |
| `cólico` / `calambre` | KOH-lee-koh / kah-LAHM-breh | cramping / cramp | Colic, obstruction, muscle |
| `fuerte` / `leve` | FWER-teh / LEH-beh | strong / mild | Severity without a number |
| `falta de aire` | FAHL-tah deh AH-ee-reh | shortness of breath | Say it as one chunk |
| `mareado` | mah-reh-AH-doh | dizzy, lightheaded | Also used for nauseated |
| `náuseas` / `vómito` | NOW-seh-ahs / BOH-mee-toh | nausea / vomit | |
| `fiebre` / `escalofríos` | FYEH-breh / es-kah-loh-FREE-ohs | fever / chills | |
| `hinchazón` | een-chah-SOHN | swelling | |
| `entumecido` / `hormigueo` | en-too-meh-SEE-doh / or-mee-GEH-oh | numb / tingling | Stroke and nerve complaints |
| `débil` | DEH-beel | weak | |

## Pointing beats grammar

The most reliable pain assessment you can do alone has no sentences in it. Touch or hover over a region and ask `¿aquí?` (ah-KEE, here). Watch the face, not the mouth. Then `¿y aquí?` (ee ah-KEE, and here). You have just mapped the tenderness without conjugating anything.

Two more that pay for themselves: `¿Le duele al respirar?` (does it hurt when you breathe) and `¿Se corre el dolor?` (koh-reh, does the pain travel). Radiation and pleuritic quality are exactly what the nurse needs before an ECG decision.

> **On shift:** `mareado` is used loosely. It can mean lightheaded, spinning, or sick to the stomach. When you hear it, flag it for the nurse rather than translating it in your head as dizzy, because the difference between vertigo and presyncope changes the workup.
keyPoints: `dolor de` plus a body part, and `me duele` / `¿le duele?`, cover most of pain vocabulary.
Point and ask `¿aquí?` to map tenderness with no grammar at all.
`presión` and `opresión` are the classic cardiac descriptions; report those words verbatim.
`falta de aire` is shortness of breath; `entumecido` and `hormigueo` are numb and tingling.
`mareado` is vague and can mean dizzy, spinning, or nauseated; hand it to the nurse rather than interpreting it.

checks.q: A patient with chest discomfort says `siento presión`. Why does that word matter?
choices: It means the pain is mild
It means pressure, the classic description of cardiac chest pain, and should be reported verbatim
It means the pain is only positional
checks.why: `presión` and `opresión` describe a squeezing, heavy quality typical of ischemic chest pain. Reporting the patient's own word preserves the description; translating it loosely as discomfort loses the finding.

checks.q: How do you ask whether the pain is in one specific spot you are pointing to?
checks.why: `¿Le duele aquí?` means does it hurt here and pairs with pointing. The others ask how long, how much, and whether there is pain at all, none of which localize anything.

checks.q: A patient tells you `tengo falta de aire`. What is she reporting?
checks.why: `falta de aire` is the standard everyday phrase for shortness of breath and is treated as one chunk. It is a respiratory complaint that goes to the nurse immediately, along with a pulse oximetry reading.

lessons.title: The triage questions and the answers you will hear
lessons.body:
## The seven questions

Full history goes through an interpreter. But you will be in rooms where the interpreter is still ringing and the nurse needs a direction, and these seven questions get asked in every triage in the country. Knowing them lets you follow the interpreted conversation instead of staring at it, and lets you pick up an urgent answer the moment it lands.

| Spanish | Say it | Meaning | Answer you expect |
|---|---|---|---|
| `¿Qué le pasa?` | keh leh PAH-sah | What is going on? | A complaint, often one word |
| `¿Desde cuándo?` | DES-deh KWAN-doh | Since when? | A time expression, see below |
| `¿Tiene alergias?` | TYEH-neh ah-LEHR-hyahs | Do you have allergies? | `no` or a drug name |
| `¿Toma medicamentos?` | TOH-mah meh-dee-kah-MEN-tohs | Do you take medications? | A list, or a bag of bottles |
| `¿Está embarazada?` | es-TAH em-bah-rah-SAH-dah | Are you pregnant? | `sí`, `no`, `no sé` |
| `¿Tiene diabetes, presión alta o asma?` | dyah-BEH-tehs, preh-SYON AHL-tah, AHS-mah | Diabetes, high blood pressure, or asthma? | Any combination |
| `¿Ha tenido cirugías?` | ah teh-NEE-doh see-roo-HEE-ahs | Have you had surgeries? | A year and a body part |

Two add-ons worth having: `¿Fuma?` (FOO-mah, do you smoke) and `¿Cuándo fue su última regla?` (OOL-tee-mah REH-glah, when was your last period). `la regla` is the everyday word; `la menstruación` is the formal one.

## The answers

Understanding is harder than speaking, because the patient will not slow down. These are the answers that actually come back.

| Spanish | Say it | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `sí` / `no` / `no sé` | see / noh / noh seh | yes / no / I do not know |
| `a veces` | ah BEH-sehs | sometimes |
| `un poco` / `mucho` | oon POH-koh / MOO-choh | a little / a lot |
| `desde anoche` | DES-deh ah-NOH-cheh | since last night |
| `esta mañana` | ES-tah mah-NYAH-nah | this morning |
| `hace dos días` | AH-seh dohs DEE-ahs | two days ago |
| `hace una semana` / `un mes` | AH-seh OO-nah seh-MAH-nah / oon mehs | a week ago / a month ago |
| `ayer` / `hoy` | ah-YEHR / oy | yesterday / today |
| `de repente` | deh reh-PEN-teh | suddenly |
| `poco a poco` | POH-koh ah POH-koh | gradually |
| `peor` / `mejor` / `igual` | peh-OR / meh-HOR / ee-GWAL | worse / better / the same |

`hace` plus a length of time is the single most useful pattern here: `hace` means ago. `hace tres horas` is three hours ago, which for chest pain or stroke symptoms is the number the whole workup turns on.

> **Key:** `de repente` versus `poco a poco` is sudden versus gradual onset. Sudden onset of the worst headache, chest pain, or back pain is a different emergency than the same pain that crept up over a week.

## False friends that change care

These words look like English words and mean something else. Each one has sent a patient down the wrong path.

| Spanish | It actually means | Not | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|---|
| `embarazada` | pregnant | embarrassed | Pregnancy test, imaging, medication choices |
| `constipado` | congested, stuffy nose | constipated | Do not chart a bowel complaint for a cold |
| `intoxicado` | poisoned, food poisoning | drunk | A GI or toxic exposure, not an alcohol problem |
| `sano` | healthy | sane | A patient saying `estoy sano` is denying medical history |
| `molestar` | to bother | to molest | `¿Le molesta?` is does it bother you |
| `once` | eleven | once, one time | Pill counts |
| `contestar` | to answer | to contest | |
| `atender` | to care for, to see to | to attend | `ya lo van a atender` means they will see him soon |

The embarrassed word is `avergonzado`. Constipated is `estreñido` (es-treh-NYEE-doh). Drunk is `borracho` or `ebrio`.

> **Trap:** `constipado` is the one that slips through most often, because it arrives inside a sentence about feeling sick and sounds exactly like the English. If a patient says `estoy constipado` and also has a cough and a runny nose, they mean congested.
keyPoints: Seven triage questions cover complaint, duration, allergies, medications, pregnancy, chronic disease, and surgeries.
`hace` plus a time means ago; `hace tres horas` is the number that drives stroke and chest pain decisions.
`de repente` is sudden onset, `poco a poco` is gradual. Report which one you heard.
False friends that matter: `embarazada` is pregnant, `constipado` is congested, `intoxicado` is poisoned, `sano` is healthy, `once` is eleven.
`la regla` is the everyday word for menstrual period.

checks.q: A patient with a cough and runny nose says `estoy constipado`. What does he mean?
checks.why: `constipado` means nasal congestion. Constipated is `estreñido`. Charting a bowel complaint here sends the workup in a direction the patient never described.

checks.q: A patient with left-sided weakness answers `hace dos horas` when asked about onset. Why does that answer matter most?
choices: It tells you the pain is mild
It establishes the last known well time, which drives stroke treatment decisions
It confirms the symptoms are chronic
checks.why: `hace dos horas` is two hours ago. Time of onset determines thrombolytic and thrombectomy eligibility, so it is the highest-value number in the encounter. It neither confirms nor excludes stroke by itself.

checks.q: Which question asks about allergies?
checks.why: `¿Tiene alergias?` is do you have allergies. The others ask about medications, past surgeries, and the chief complaint. All four belong in triage, but only one of them prevents you from giving a drug that harms the patient.

lessons.title: Vitals, needles, and the monitor
lessons.body:
## Announce, then command

Every hands-on task follows the same two-beat rhythm: `Voy a...` to say what is coming, then a one-word command for what the patient should do. Announcing first prevents the flinch, and a flinch during a blood draw or a 12-lead costs you the sample or the tracing. Commands for `usted` mostly end in **-e** or **-a**; memorize them as sounds.

## Vital signs

| Spanish | Say it | Meaning | When to use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Voy a tomarle los signos vitales.` | boy ah toh-MAR-leh lohs SEEG-nohs bee-TAH-lehs | I am going to take your vital signs. | Opening line |
| `Voy a tomarle la presión.` | boy ah toh-MAR-leh lah preh-SYON | I am going to take your blood pressure. | Cuff |
| `Le va a apretar el brazo.` | leh bah ah ah-preh-TAR el BRAH-soh | It is going to squeeze your arm. | Prevents alarm |
| `Relaje el brazo.` | reh-LAH-heh el BRAH-soh | Relax your arm. | Cuff, IV |
| `Abra la boca.` | AH-brah lah BOH-kah | Open your mouth. | Oral temperature |
| `Es solo para medir el oxígeno.` | es SOH-loh PAH-rah meh-DEER el ok-SEE-heh-noh | It is only to measure oxygen. | Pulse ox clip |
| `No duele.` | noh DWEH-leh | It does not hurt. | Pulse ox, ECG, cuff |

## Positioning

| Spanish | Say it | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `Siéntese.` | SYEN-teh-seh | Sit down. |
| `Acuéstese.` | ah-KWES-teh-seh | Lie down. |
| `Dese vuelta.` | DEH-seh BWEL-tah | Turn over. |
| `De lado.` | deh LAH-doh | On your side. |
| `Levante el brazo.` | leh-BAHN-teh el BRAH-soh | Raise your arm. |
| `No se mueva.` | noh seh MWEH-bah | Do not move. |

## The blood draw

| Spanish | Say it | Meaning | When to use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Voy a sacarle sangre.` | boy ah sah-KAR-leh SAHN-greh | I am going to draw your blood. | Announce first, always |
| `Apriete el puño.` | ah-PRYEH-teh el POO-nyoh | Make a fist. | After the tourniquet |
| `Abra la mano.` | AH-brah lah MAH-noh | Open your hand. | Once flash is in the hub |
| `Un pinchazo.` | oon peen-CHAH-soh | A little stick. | The half second before |
| `Ya casi.` | yah KAH-see | Almost done. | Mid-draw |
| `Ya terminé.` | yah ter-mee-NEH | I am finished. | |
| `Haga presión aquí.` | AH-gah preh-SYON ah-KEE | Press here. | Handing over the gauze |

> **Key:** `Un pinchazo` just before the needle does more for cooperation than any other word here. An unannounced stick makes the arm jump, and a jumped arm is a blown vein.

## The 12-lead and the monitor

| Spanish | Say it | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `Voy a ponerle unos parches en el pecho.` | boy ah poh-NEHR-leh OO-nohs PAR-chehs en el PEH-choh | I am going to put some patches on your chest. |
| `Necesito bajarle la bata.` | neh-seh-SEE-toh bah-HAR-leh lah BAH-tah | I need to lower your gown. |
| `Es para ver el corazón.` | es PAH-rah behr el koh-rah-SOHN | It is to look at your heart. |
| `No hable, relájese.` | noh AH-bleh, reh-LAH-heh-seh | Do not talk, relax. |
| `Respire normal.` | res-PEE-reh nor-MAHL | Breathe normally. |
| `Son diez segundos.` | sohn dyess seh-GOON-dohs | It is ten seconds. |
| `Voy a conectarle el monitor.` | boy ah koh-nek-TAR-leh el moh-nee-TOR | I am going to connect you to the monitor. |
| `Si suena, es normal.` | see SWEH-nah, es nor-MAHL | If it beeps, that is normal. |

For breathing instructions: `Respire profundo` (res-PEE-reh proh-FOON-doh) is take a deep breath, `Otra vez` (OH-trah behs) is again, and `Aguante` (ah-GWAN-teh) is hold it.

> **On shift:** Chest exposure for a 12-lead is where modesty collides with speed, most often with older women. Close the curtain first, say what you need, keep a sheet over everything not in use, and offer a female staff member when one is available.
keyPoints: Two-beat rhythm: announce with `Voy a...`, then a one-word command.
Blood draw sequence: `Voy a sacarle sangre`, `Apriete el puño`, `Un pinchazo`, `Abra la mano`, `Haga presión aquí`.
`Un pinchazo` just before the needle prevents the flinch that blows the vein.
12-lead: `Voy a ponerle unos parches en el pecho`, `No hable, relájese`, `Son diez segundos`.
Announce chest exposure, curtain first, sheet over everything not in use, and offer a female staff member when you can.

checks.q: You have the tourniquet on and the vein selected. What do you say?
checks.why: `Apriete el puño` is make a fist, which distends the vein. `Abra la mano` comes after you are in the vein. The others are positioning and breathing commands unrelated to the draw.

checks.q: Which set of phrases fits a 12-lead ECG?
choices: `Voy a ponerle unos parches en el pecho` and `No hable, relájese`
`Abra la boca` and `Debajo de la lengua`
checks.why: Patches on the chest and stay quiet and still are exactly the two things a 12-lead needs, since talking and muscle movement create artifact. The other sets belong to phlebotomy, an oral temperature, and repositioning.

checks.q: What is the clinical reason to say `Un pinchazo` before you stick?
choices: It tells the patient a brief stick is coming so the arm does not jump and blow the vein
It means the draw will not hurt
It is how you ask permission to draw
checks.why: It is a warning, not consent and not a promise of no pain. An unannounced needle produces a reflex withdrawal that costs the vein and the sample. Consent for the draw is part of the interpreted conversation.

lessons.title: Urine samples, splints, and wounds
lessons.body:
## The specimen conversation

A urine sample is the task most often ruined by a language gap, because it is entirely instructions and the patient performs it alone in a bathroom. A contaminated specimen means a repeat collection or, worse, a treated infection the patient never had.

| Spanish | Say it | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `Necesito una muestra de orina.` | neh-seh-SEE-toh OO-nah MWES-trah deh oh-REE-nah | I need a urine sample. |
| `¿Puede orinar ahora?` | PWEH-deh oh-ree-NAR ah-OH-rah | Can you urinate now? |
| `Aquí está el vaso.` | ah-KEE es-TAH el BAH-soh | Here is the cup. |
| `No toque adentro del vaso.` | noh TOH-keh ah-DEN-troh del BAH-soh | Do not touch the inside of the cup. |
| `Póngalo en la ventanilla.` | POHN-gah-loh en lah ben-tah-NEE-yah | Put it in the little window. |
| `¿Está usando toalla?` | es-TAH oo-SAHN-doh toh-AH-yah | Are you using a pad? |

The clean catch, simplified to three steps, is all you need:

1. `Límpiese con estas toallitas.` (LEEM-pyeh-seh kon ES-tahs toh-ah-YEE-tahs) Clean yourself with these wipes.
2. `De adelante hacia atrás.` (deh ah-deh-LAHN-teh AH-syah ah-TRAHS) From front to back.
3. `Empiece a orinar, luego llene el vaso.` (em-PYEH-seh ah oh-ree-NAR, LWEH-goh YEH-neh el BAH-soh) Start urinating, then fill the cup.

> **Trap:** Handing over a cup and pointing at the bathroom is not instruction. Front to back, and midstream rather than first stream, are the two steps that make the specimen usable, and both get skipped when the language is hard.

## Splints and orthopedic holds

| Spanish | Say it | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `Le voy a poner una férula.` | leh boy ah poh-NEHR OO-nah FEH-roo-lah | I am going to put a splint on you. |
| `Es para que no se mueva.` | es PAH-rah keh noh seh MWEH-bah | It is to keep it from moving. |
| `Dígame si está muy apretado.` | DEE-gah-meh see es-TAH mooy ah-preh-TAH-doh | Tell me if it is too tight. |
| `¿Siente los dedos?` | SYEN-teh lohs DEH-dohs | Can you feel your fingers or toes? |
| `Mueva los dedos.` | MWEH-bah lohs DEH-dohs | Move your fingers or toes. |
| `No apoye el pie.` | noh ah-POH-yeh el pyeh | Do not put weight on that foot. |
| `Manténgalo en alto.` | mahn-TEN-gah-loh en AHL-toh | Keep it elevated. |
| `Voy a ponerle hielo.` | boy ah poh-NEHR-leh YEH-loh | I am going to put ice on it. |
| `Voy a ponerle un cabestrillo.` | oon kah-bes-TREE-yoh | I am going to put on a sling. |

`¿Siente los dedos?` and `Mueva los dedos.` are your circulation, sensation, and motion check before and after every splint. Those two sentences are worth more than the rest of the table, because a splint that was fine at application and numb twenty minutes later is the finding that prevents a compartment problem from being missed.

## Wounds

| Spanish | Say it | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `la herida` | lah eh-REE-dah | the wound |
| `Voy a limpiar la herida.` | boy ah leem-PYAR lah eh-REE-dah | I am going to clean the wound. |
| `Le va a arder un poco.` | leh bah ah AR-der oon POH-koh | It is going to sting a little. |
| `Voy a ponerle un vendaje.` | oon ben-DAH-heh | I am going to put on a bandage. |
| `Necesita puntos.` | neh-seh-SEE-tah POON-tohs | You need stitches. |
| `¿Cuándo fue su última vacuna del tétano?` | TEH-tah-noh | When was your last tetanus shot? |
| `No moje el vendaje.` | noh MOH-heh el ben-DAH-heh | Do not get the bandage wet. |
| `Haga presión, fuerte.` | AH-gah preh-SYON, FWER-teh | Press hard. |

`Necesita puntos` is a statement about the plan, so it belongs to the provider and the interpreter, not to you. `Le va a arder un poco` is honest and worth saying: warning someone about a sting keeps them still, while promising no pain and then causing it costs you every instruction after that.

> **On shift:** Tetanus status is a real clinical question that goes through the interpreter, but the word `tétano` is close enough to English that patients often answer it before the interpreter connects. Hold the answer, then confirm it once the interpreter is on.
keyPoints: A urine sample is pure instruction: wipes, front to back, start urinating then fill the cup.
`No toque adentro del vaso` prevents the contamination that forces a recollection.
Splints: `Dígame si está muy apretado`, `¿Siente los dedos?`, `Mueva los dedos`, `Manténgalo en alto`.
Warn honestly with `Le va a arder un poco` rather than promising it will not hurt.
Plan statements like `Necesita puntos` belong to the provider through an interpreter.

checks.q: Which two instructions make a urine specimen usable?
choices: Drink water first and fill the cup completely
Wipe front to back, and catch midstream rather than the first stream
Use the bathroom nearest the room and hurry
Wash hands and label the cup yourself
checks.why: Front-to-back cleaning and a midstream catch are what reduce periurethral contamination. Volume, bathroom choice, and hand washing are fine but do not change whether the culture is interpretable.

checks.q: You finished applying a forearm splint. Which pair of phrases checks it?
checks.why: Sensation and motion in the fingers is the neurovascular check distal to the splint. Fist and open hand are phlebotomy commands, the breathing pair belongs to lung sounds, and positioning commands check nothing.

checks.q: Before irrigating a laceration, the most useful thing to say is:
checks.why: Irrigation stings, so an honest warning keeps the patient still and preserves your credibility. Saying it does not hurt is false and costs you cooperation. Stitches are a provider decision and the bandage instruction comes later.

lessons.title: Comfort, orientation, and the family in the room
lessons.body:
## What a scared person needs to hear

Most of what makes an emergency department frightening is not pain, it is not knowing: where you are, what is happening, how long, and whether anyone is coming. Four short sentences solve most of that, and all four are safely inside a tech's lane.

| Spanish | Say it | Meaning | When to use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Está en el hospital.` | es-TAH en el os-pee-TAHL | You are in the hospital. | Confusion, waking up, post-ictal |
| `Está seguro.` / `segura.` | es-TAH seh-GOO-roh / -rah | You are safe. | After an assault, a fall, a seizure |
| `Ya viene el doctor.` / `la doctora.` | yah BYEH-neh el dok-TOR | The doctor is coming. | Only when true |
| `Estoy aquí con usted.` | es-TOY ah-KEE kon oos-TED | I am here with you. | When you cannot fix anything else |
| `¿Necesita algo?` | neh-seh-SEE-tah AHL-goh | Do you need anything? | Every time you pass the room |
| `¿Quiere agua?` | KYEH-reh AH-gwah | Do you want water? | Only if the patient is cleared to drink |
| `¿Quiere una manta?` | OO-nah MAHN-tah | Do you want a blanket? | Almost always yes |
| `¿Quiere llamar a alguien?` | KYEH-reh yah-MAR ah AHL-gyen | Do you want to call someone? | Alone, undocumented, or scared |
| `¿Necesita ir al baño?` | eer al BAH-nyoh | Do you need the bathroom? | Before anyone gets up unassisted |
| `Voy a apagar la luz.` | boy ah ah-pah-GAR lah loos | I am going to turn off the light. | Headache, photophobia |

`¿Quiere agua?` has a condition attached. Anyone who may go to surgery, has an altered mental status, or has not passed a swallow screen after stroke symptoms stays nothing by mouth. Ask the nurse first, then offer.

## The sentence you do not say

`Todo va a estar bien` means everything is going to be fine. It is warm, it is instinctive, and it is a promise about an outcome you do not know.

Do not say it when the patient is critically ill, when a family is waiting for news, when a resuscitation is happening, or when you have any reason to think the news will be bad. A promise that fails is remembered for years, and it destroys the credibility of every true thing you said before it.

Say instead what is actually true: `Estamos cuidándole` (es-TAH-mohs kwee-DAHN-doh-leh, we are taking care of you), `Estoy aquí con usted`, or `El doctor le va a explicar` (the doctor is going to explain it to you).

> **Key:** Comfort the person, never predict the outcome. `Estoy aquí con usted` is always true. `Todo va a estar bien` sometimes is not.

## Family is not a visitor problem

In many Latino families the expectation is that someone stays. Three generations in a small room is normal, not an overflow. Fighting that costs you far more than it gains, and the family is frequently your best source of baseline: what she is normally like, what she took this morning, when she last ate.

A few things that make it work:

- Find the **spokesperson**, usually the one who answers first, and route updates through that person.
- Adult children often want to protect a parent from bad news. That is a real cultural pattern and it is not your call to override at the bedside. Tell the nurse, who will bring it to the provider.
- `¿Es usted familiar?` (fah-mee-LYAR) is are you family. `¿Quién es el que decide?` is who makes the decisions.
- Immigration status is never your question and never belongs in the chart. Fear of it keeps people out of emergency departments until they are much sicker, and it is a reason to be visibly unbothered by it, not curious.

## Folk remedies and folk illnesses

You will hear `susto` (fright sickness), `empacho` (blocked stomach), or `mal de ojo` (evil eye), and you will hear about teas and herbs: `manzanilla` (chamomile), `sábila` (aloe), `té de...` for almost anything.

Do not argue with the term and do not roll your eyes. Do make sure the herbal and home remedies get into the medication history through the interpreter, because some of them interact with real drugs and almost none of them get volunteered when a patient expects to be mocked.

> **On shift:** Simply saying `permítame` (per-MEE-tah-meh, allow me) as you step into a crowded room, instead of announcing that only two visitors are allowed, gets you to the bedside without a confrontation nine times out of ten.
keyPoints: `Está en el hospital`, `Está seguro`, `Estoy aquí con usted` orient and calm without promising anything.
Do not say `Todo va a estar bien` to a critically ill patient or a waiting family; say `Estamos cuidándole` instead.
Check nothing-by-mouth status with the nurse before offering `¿Quiere agua?`.
Family presence is expected; find the spokesperson and use the family for baseline history.
Immigration status is never your question and never goes in the chart; folk remedies do belong in the medication history.

checks.q: A family is waiting for news on a critically ill patient. Which is the wrong thing to say?
checks.why: `Todo va a estar bien` promises an outcome nobody can guarantee, and when it fails it invalidates everything else you said. The other three are true, comforting, and stay inside what a tech actually knows.

checks.q: A patient with slurred speech and facial droop asks for water in Spanish. What do you do?
choices: Tell the nurse and hold all oral intake until a swallow screen is done
Give ice chips instead, which are always safe
checks.why: Stroke symptoms mean aspiration risk until a swallow screen is passed, and ice chips are still oral intake. The decision belongs to the nurse, not to the tech or the family, no matter how reasonable the request sounds.

checks.q: A patient mentions she has been drinking `té de manzanilla` and taking `sábila` at home. What should happen with that?
choices: Ignore it; herbal remedies are not medications
Tell her to stop using them
Make sure it reaches the medication history through the interpreter
checks.why: Herbal products can interact with prescribed drugs and belong in the medication history. Dismissing or correcting the patient guarantees that the next remedy, possibly one that matters more, never gets mentioned at all.

lessons.title: Red-flag Spanish: recognize it and move
lessons.body:
## The one-way vocabulary

Everything else in this module is two-way. This lesson is one-way: you never need to say these sentences, you need to recognize them in under a second, out of a hallway, from a family member who is talking too fast, and then move.

Treat this list the way you treat a monitor alarm. The response is the same every time: get the nurse, now, and say what you heard in the patient's words.

| What you hear | Say it | It means | Do this |
|---|---|---|---|
| `No puedo respirar.` | noh PWEH-doh res-pee-RAR | I cannot breathe. | Nurse now, pulse ox, sit them up |
| `Me duele el pecho.` | meh DWEH-leh el PEH-choh | My chest hurts. | Nurse now, 12-lead within 10 minutes |
| `Me falta el aire.` | meh FAHL-tah el AH-ee-reh | I cannot get air. | Same as cannot breathe |
| `Se desmayó.` | seh des-mah-YOH | He or she fainted. | Nurse now, vitals, glucose |
| `Está convulsionando.` | kon-bool-syoh-NAHN-doh | He or she is seizing. | Nurse now, protect the head, note the time |
| `Una convulsión.` | OO-nah kon-bool-SYON | A seizure. | Same |
| `Está embarazada y está sangrando.` | em-bah-rah-SAH-dah ee sahn-GRAHN-doh | She is pregnant and bleeding. | Nurse now, do not leave her alone |
| `Tomó pastillas.` | toh-MOH pas-TEE-yahs | He or she took pills. | Nurse now, get the bottles, count |
| `No siente el brazo.` | noh SYEN-teh el BRAH-soh | He or she cannot feel their arm. | Stroke pathway, last known well time |
| `No puede hablar.` | noh PWEH-deh ah-BLAR | He or she cannot speak. | Same |
| `Se cayó.` | seh kah-YOH | He or she fell. | Nurse; ask about blood thinners |
| `Se está muriendo.` | seh es-TAH moo-RYEN-doh | He or she is dying. | Go look yourself, immediately |
| `Ayúdeme.` / `Auxilio.` | ah-YOO-deh-meh / owk-SEE-lyoh | Help me. / Help. | Go look yourself |
| `Está sangrando mucho.` | sahn-GRAHN-doh MOO-choh | He or she is bleeding a lot. | Direct pressure, nurse |
| `Se está ahogando.` | seh es-TAH ah-oh-GAHN-doh | He or she is choking. | Immediate, do not wait for the nurse |

> **Key:** You are not triaging these. You are relaying them. Repeat the patient's own words to the nurse, do not summarize them into something softer.

## Three words that do the most work

If you learn only three items here, learn these, because each one starts a timed pathway.

- `pecho` plus `dolor` or `presión`. A 12-lead ECG within `10 minutes` of arrival is the standard for chest pain that might be cardiac. Every minute you spend deciding whether you heard right is a minute off that clock.
- `no puedo respirar` or `falta de aire`. Get a pulse oximetry number before you get anything else. A number beats a description in every handoff.
- `no siente` or `no puede hablar` or `no puede mover`. Any of these is a stroke pathway, and the question that follows is always **when was he or she last normal**: `¿Cuándo fue la última vez que estaba bien?`

## Say the situation, not a diagnosis

When you relay it, give three things: who, the exact words, and how long. "Room 12, the daughter says `se desmayó` about ten minutes ago in the lobby." That is complete. "Room 12 might be a syncope" is a diagnosis you are not making and it strips out the timing.

If you are not sure what you heard, say that too. `No entiendo, un momento` (noh en-TYEN-doh, I do not understand, one moment) is a perfectly good sentence, and it is far better than guessing. Then get the interpreter or get the nurse.

> **Trap:** The most dangerous word in this lesson is a maybe. A family member saying something urgent and fast that you only half-caught is still an alarm. Half-caught urgency gets escalated exactly like fully-understood urgency.

## While you wait for help

These are the few things you can say back that do not commit you to anything: `Ya voy` (yah boy, I am coming), `Ya viene la enfermera` (the nurse is coming), `Un momento`, and `Estoy aquí`. Then do the physical thing that matters: sit them up, put the pulse ox on, hold pressure, or put your hand on the bed rail and stay.
keyPoints: This vocabulary is recognition only; the response to any of it is get the nurse and repeat the patient's exact words.
`dolor` or `presión` in the `pecho` starts the 10-minute 12-lead clock.
`no puedo respirar` and `falta de aire` mean get a pulse oximetry number first.
`no siente`, `no puede hablar`, `no puede mover` are the stroke pathway; the next question is when they were last normal.
Half-understood urgency gets escalated exactly like fully-understood urgency.

checks.q: A woman in the hallway says her husband `tomó pastillas`. What is she telling you?
choices: He took pills, which in this context is an ingestion or overdose
checks.why: `tomó` is past tense, he took, and paired with urgency it means an ingestion. The daily-medication version is `toma pastillas`, present tense. The next steps are the nurse and the actual bottles for a pill count.

checks.q: You half-hear a family member say something with `pecho` and `duele` while you are wheeling a stretcher past. What do you do?
choices: Finish the transport, then go back and clarify
Find an interpreter before doing anything
Stop, get the nurse, and report exactly the words you heard
Ask the family member to write it down
checks.why: Chest pain starts a 10-minute ECG clock, so partial understanding is still an alarm. Waiting for transport or for an interpreter burns the clock, and the correct escalation is to hand the nurse the exact words and let her assess.

checks.q: A patient's son says `no puede hablar` about his mother. Beyond getting the nurse, what is the single most valuable piece of information to obtain?
choices: When she was last known to be normal
checks.why: Inability to speak is a stroke presentation, and last known well time drives thrombolytic and thrombectomy eligibility. A pain score is not applicable, and insurance and language are real but do not change the time-critical decision.

cards.front: Who pays for a medical interpreter, and can a hospital ask the patient to bring one?
cards.back: The hospital pays. Under Title VI and ACA Section 1557, language assistance is free to the patient, and a facility taking federal funds may not require the patient to supply their own interpreter.

cards.front: Name three things you may NOT do in Spanish without a qualified interpreter.
cards.back: Take a history, obtain consent for a procedure, and give discharge instructions. Add: allergies and medication list for the chart, results, and any refusal or AMA conversation.

cards.front: What is an ad hoc interpreter and why is it a problem?
cards.back: Any untrained interpreter: family, friend, or untested bilingual staff. They produce far more clinically significant errors than trained interpreters, skewed toward omissions that make the patient sound better than they are.

cards.front: When, if ever, may a child interpret?
cards.back: Never for non-emergent care. The only exception anywhere is a true emergency where seconds matter and no interpreter can be reached; get qualified help immediately after and document it.

cards.front: How do you phrase a question when an interpreter is on the line?
cards.back: Speak directly to the patient in the first person while looking at them: "When did the pain start?" Not "Ask her when the pain started." One idea per sentence, then pause.

cards.front: What three things do you document about interpreter use?
cards.back: That an interpreter was used, the modality (in person, video, or phone), and the interpreter's ID number.

cards.front: Spanish for: The interpreter is coming.
cards.back: `Ya viene el intérprete.` Say it yah BYEH-neh el een-TEHR-preh-teh. Pair it with `Un momento, por favor` (oon mo-MEN-toh por fah-BOR) while you dial.

cards.front: What are the five Spanish vowel sounds?
cards.back: `a` ah as in father, `e` eh as in bet, `i` ee as in see, `o` oh short and flat, `u` oo as in food. Each letter has exactly one sound, every time.

cards.front: How do you pronounce `j`, and `g` before e or i?
cards.back: Both are an English h made further back in the throat. `ojo` is OH-hoh, `hija` is EE-hah, `alergia` is ah-LEHR-hyah, `cirugía` is see-roo-HEE-ah.

cards.front: How are `ll`, `ñ`, and `h` pronounced?
cards.back: `ll` is a y: `pastillas` is pas-TEE-yahs. `ñ` is ny: `año` is AH-nyoh. `h` is always silent: `hospital` is os-pee-TAHL, `herida` is eh-REE-dah.

cards.front: State the two default stress rules in Spanish.
cards.back: Word ends in a vowel, n, or s: stress the second-to-last syllable (`pecho`, PEH-choh). Ends in any other consonant: stress the last (`dolor`, doh-LOR).

cards.front: What does a written accent mark tell you?
cards.back: Stress falls exactly there, overriding both default rules. `corazón` is koh-rah-SOHN, `médico` is MEH-dee-koh, `presión` is preh-SYON.

cards.front: Clinically, why does `tomo` versus `tomó` matter?
cards.back: `tomo` (TOH-moh) is I take, a home medication. `tomó` (toh-MOH) is he or she took, which in an ingestion history is an overdose. One syllable of stress separates them.

cards.front: How is `z`, and `c` before e or i, pronounced in Latin American Spanish?
cards.back: As an s. `cero` is SEH-roh, `corazón` is koh-rah-SOHN, `cirugía` is see-roo-HEE-ah.

cards.front: Spanish for: Hello, my name is... I am an emergency technician.
cards.back: `Hola, me llamo...` (OH-lah, meh YAH-moh). `Soy técnico de emergencias` (soy TEK-nee-koh deh eh-mer-HEN-syahs), or `técnica` if you are a woman.

cards.front: `usted` or `tú` with an adult patient, and why?
cards.back: Always `usted`. It is the formal, respectful form. `tú` with an adult, especially an elder, sounds like talking down to a child and costs trust immediately.

cards.front: Which titles do you use with adult patients?
cards.back: `señor` for a man, `señora` for an adult woman, `señorita` for a young woman. `Don` and `Doña` plus a first name are a warm high-respect form common with older patients.

cards.front: What do `Voy a...` and `¿Puedo...?` mean, and how are they used together?
cards.back: `Voy a...` is I am going to, announcing the task. `¿Puedo...?` is may I, asking permission. Announce, ask, then act: `Voy a levantarle la manga. ¿Está bien?`

cards.front: Spanish for: Excuse me / with your permission.
cards.back: `Con permiso` (kon per-MEE-soh). Use it entering a room, reaching across a patient, or moving a blanket. `Permítame` (per-MEE-tah-meh) is allow me, for getting through a crowded room.

cards.front: How do you ask for the two patient identifiers in Spanish?
cards.back: `¿Me dice su nombre completo?` (meh DEE-seh soo NOM-breh kom-PLEH-toh) and `¿Su fecha de nacimiento?` (soo FEH-chah deh nah-see-MYEN-toh). Open questions, never a leading yes-or-no.

cards.front: Why does a Spanish name often not match the wristband order?
cards.back: Spanish names usually carry two surnames, father's then mother's, as in María Elena García Rivera. Registration systems reorder or truncate them. Confirm with date of birth before assuming wrong patient.

cards.front: Count 0 to 10 in Spanish.
cards.back: `cero, uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco, seis, siete, ocho, nueve, diez`. SEH-roh, OO-noh, dohs, trehs, KWAH-troh, SEEN-koh, says, SYEH-teh, OH-choh, NWEH-beh, dyess.

cards.front: What are 11 through 15 in Spanish?
cards.back: `once, doce, trece, catorce, quince`: OHN-seh, DOH-seh, TREH-seh, kah-TOR-seh, KEEN-seh. Remember `once` is eleven, not the English word once.

cards.front: Name the tens from 30 to 100 in Spanish.
cards.back: `treinta, cuarenta, cincuenta, sesenta, setenta, ochenta, noventa, cien`. Join with `y`: `treinta y dos` is 32, `sesenta y ocho` is 68.

cards.front: How do you ask age in Spanish, for an adult and for an infant?
cards.back: `¿Cuántos años tiene?` (KWAN-tohs AH-nyohs TYEH-neh) for years. `¿Cuántos meses tiene?` (MEH-sehs) for months, which is what you need for infant dosing.

cards.front: Why must you always ask `¿en libras o en kilos?`
cards.back: Patients from Latin America usually answer in kilos, US-raised patients in pounds. Charting 70 kilos as 70 pounds is about an 84-pound error on every weight-based dose.

cards.front: Spanish for: From zero to ten, how much does it hurt?
cards.back: `¿Del cero al diez, cuánto le duele?` (del SEH-roh al dyess, KWAN-toh leh DWEH-leh). Anchor it with `Cero es nada, diez es lo peor` and hold up ten fingers.

cards.front: A patient says `tengo treinta y ocho` about temperature. What is that in Fahrenheit?
cards.back: 38 C, which is 100.4 F. Patients outside the US report temperature in Celsius; 38 C is the standard fever threshold.

cards.front: What is the difference between `dolor` and `me duele`?
cards.back: `dolor` is the noun, pain: `dolor de pecho` is chest pain. `me duele` is the verb, it hurts me. You ask `¿le duele?`; plural subjects take `duelen`.

cards.front: Spanish for chest, back, belly, and throat.
cards.back: `el pecho` (PEH-choh), `la espalda` (es-PAHL-dah), `la barriga` or `el estómago` (bah-REE-gah, es-TOH-mah-goh), `la garganta` (gar-GAHN-tah).

cards.front: Spanish for shoulder, elbow, wrist, knee, and ankle.
cards.back: `el hombro` (OM-broh), `el codo` (KOH-doh), `la muñeca` (moo-NYEH-kah), `la rodilla` (roh-DEE-yah), `el tobillo` (toh-BEE-yoh).

cards.front: Which Spanish pain words suggest a cardiac quality, and what do you do with them?
cards.back: `presión` and `opresión`, pressure and tightness. Report the patient's exact word to the nurse rather than softening it to discomfort.

cards.front: What do `ardor`, `punzante`, and `cólico` describe?
cards.back: `ardor` is burning (ar-DOR), `punzante` is stabbing (poon-SAHN-teh), `cólico` is cramping (KOH-lee-koh). Quality of pain, which narrows the differential.

cards.front: How does a Spanish-speaking patient say shortness of breath?
cards.back: `falta de aire` (FAHL-tah deh AH-ee-reh), literally lack of air. Also `me falta el aire`. Treat it as one chunk and get a pulse oximetry reading.

cards.front: What do `entumecido` and `hormigueo` mean, and why do they matter?
cards.back: Numb (en-too-meh-SEE-doh) and tingling (or-mee-GEH-oh). Both are neurologic complaints that can be part of a stroke presentation, so they go to the nurse with a time of onset.

cards.front: Why should you hand `mareado` to the nurse rather than translate it yourself?
cards.back: It is used loosely for lightheaded, spinning, or nauseated. Vertigo and presyncope get different workups, so the distinction has to be made by the assessing clinician, ideally through an interpreter.

cards.front: Give the Spanish for: What is going on? Since when?
cards.back: `¿Qué le pasa?` (keh leh PAH-sah) and `¿Desde cuándo?` (DES-deh KWAN-doh). Complaint and duration, the first two triage questions.

cards.front: Give the Spanish for: Do you have allergies? Do you take medications?
cards.back: `¿Tiene alergias?` (TYEH-neh ah-LEHR-hyahs) and `¿Toma medicamentos?` (TOH-mah meh-dee-kah-MEN-tohs). Both answers must be confirmed through an interpreter before charting.

cards.front: How do you ask about pregnancy, and about diabetes, hypertension, and asthma?
cards.back: `¿Está embarazada?` (es-TAH em-bah-rah-SAH-dah). `¿Tiene diabetes, presión alta o asma?` (dyah-BEH-tehs, preh-SYON AHL-tah, AHS-mah).

cards.front: What does `hace` mean in an answer like `hace dos horas`?
cards.back: Ago. `hace dos horas` is two hours ago. It is the pattern that gives you onset time, the number stroke and chest pain pathways turn on.

cards.front: What is the difference between `de repente` and `poco a poco`?
cards.back: Suddenly versus gradually. Sudden onset of a severe headache, chest pain, or back pain is a different emergency from the same pain building over days, so report which one you heard.

cards.front: What does `constipado` mean, and what is the Spanish for constipated?
cards.back: `constipado` means congested, a stuffy nose. Constipated is `estreñido` (es-treh-NYEE-doh). This false friend regularly sends a cold complaint into a GI workup.

cards.front: What do `intoxicado` and `sano` actually mean?
cards.back: `intoxicado` is poisoned, often food poisoning, not drunk (that is `borracho` or `ebrio`). `sano` is healthy, not sane. A patient saying `estoy sano` is denying medical history.

cards.front: How do you ask about the last menstrual period in everyday Spanish?
cards.back: `¿Cuándo fue su última regla?` (OOL-tee-mah REH-glah). `la regla` is the common word; `la menstruación` is formal and less often understood in casual speech.

cards.front: Spanish for: I am going to take your blood pressure. It is going to squeeze your arm.
cards.back: `Voy a tomarle la presión` (boy ah toh-MAR-leh lah preh-SYON). `Le va a apretar el brazo` (leh bah ah ah-preh-TAR el BRAH-soh). Then `Relaje el brazo`.

cards.front: Give the four positioning commands: sit, lie down, turn over, do not move.
cards.back: `Siéntese` (SYEN-teh-seh), `Acuéstese` (ah-KWES-teh-seh), `Dese vuelta` (DEH-seh BWEL-tah), `No se mueva` (noh seh MWEH-bah).

cards.front: Give the blood draw sequence in Spanish, in order.
cards.back: `Voy a sacarle sangre`, `Apriete el puño`, `Un pinchazo`, `Abra la mano`, `Ya terminé`, `Haga presión aquí`.

cards.front: What does `Apriete el puño` mean and when do you say it?
cards.back: Make a fist (ah-PRYEH-teh el POO-nyoh). Say it after the tourniquet is on, to distend the vein. Release with `Abra la mano` once you have flash.

cards.front: Why say `Un pinchazo` right before the needle?
cards.back: It warns of a brief stick so the arm does not jump. A flinch at the moment of entry blows the vein and costs you the sample. It is a warning, not consent.

cards.front: Spanish for: I am going to put some patches on your chest.
cards.back: `Voy a ponerle unos parches en el pecho` (boy ah poh-NEHR-leh OO-nohs PAR-chehs en el PEH-choh). Add `Es para ver el corazón` and `Son diez segundos`.

cards.front: What do you say to stop 12-lead artifact?
cards.back: `No hable, relájese` (noh AH-bleh, reh-LAH-heh-seh), do not talk, relax. Add `Respire normal` and `No se mueva`. Talking and muscle tension are the main artifact sources.

cards.front: Spanish for: Take a deep breath. Again. Hold it.
cards.back: `Respire profundo` (res-PEE-reh proh-FOON-doh), `Otra vez` (OH-trah behs), `Aguante` (ah-GWAN-teh).

cards.front: How do you handle chest exposure for a 12-lead on a modest patient?
cards.back: Curtain closed first, announce it (`Necesito bajarle la bata`), sheet over everything not in use, and offer a female staff member when one is available.

cards.front: Spanish for: I need a urine sample. Here is the cup.
cards.back: `Necesito una muestra de orina` (MWES-trah deh oh-REE-nah). `Aquí está el vaso` (el BAH-soh). Add `No toque adentro del vaso`.

cards.front: Give the three-step clean-catch instruction in Spanish.
cards.back: `Límpiese con estas toallitas.` `De adelante hacia atrás.` `Empiece a orinar, luego llene el vaso.` Clean with the wipes, front to back, start urinating then fill the cup.

cards.front: Spanish for: I am going to put a splint on you. Tell me if it is too tight.
cards.back: `Le voy a poner una férula` (FEH-roo-lah). `Dígame si está muy apretado` (DEE-gah-meh see es-TAH mooy ah-preh-TAH-doh).

cards.front: Which two Spanish phrases perform a neurovascular check after splinting?
cards.back: `¿Siente los dedos?` (can you feel your fingers or toes) and `Mueva los dedos` (move your fingers or toes). Sensation and motion distal to the splint.

cards.front: Spanish for: Do not put weight on that foot. Keep it elevated.
cards.back: `No apoye el pie` (noh ah-POH-yeh el pyeh). `Manténgalo en alto` (mahn-TEN-gah-loh en AHL-toh). Add `Voy a ponerle hielo` for ice.

cards.front: Spanish for wound, and for: I am going to clean the wound. It will sting a little.
cards.back: `la herida` (eh-REE-dah). `Voy a limpiar la herida.` `Le va a arder un poco` (leh bah ah AR-der oon POH-koh).

cards.front: Why is `Le va a arder un poco` better than `No duele`?
cards.back: It is true. Warning about a sting keeps the patient still and preserves your credibility; promising no pain and then causing it costs you cooperation for every instruction after.

cards.front: Give three orientation phrases for a frightened or confused patient.
cards.back: `Está en el hospital` (you are in the hospital), `Está seguro` or `segura` (you are safe), `Estoy aquí con usted` (I am here with you).

cards.front: When should you avoid saying `Todo va a estar bien`, and what do you say instead?
cards.back: Avoid it with critical illness, a waiting family, or any likely bad news. Say `Estamos cuidándole` (we are taking care of you) or `El doctor le va a explicar`.

cards.front: What must you check before offering `¿Quiere agua?`
cards.back: Nothing-by-mouth status. Possible surgery, altered mental status, or unscreened stroke symptoms all mean no oral intake, including ice chips. Ask the nurse first.

cards.front: Give three comfort offers in Spanish besides water.
cards.back: `¿Quiere una manta?` (a blanket), `¿Quiere llamar a alguien?` (to call someone), `¿Necesita ir al baño?` (the bathroom). Also `¿Necesita algo?`

cards.front: How do you handle a large family at the bedside, and what do you never ask?
cards.back: Find the spokesperson and route updates through them; use the family for baseline history. Never ask about immigration status and never put it in the chart.

cards.front: A patient says `no puedo respirar`. What is the first thing you obtain?
cards.back: A pulse oximetry number, while calling the nurse and sitting the patient up. A number travels better in a handoff than a description does.

cards.front: What do `se desmayó`, `se cayó`, and `está convulsionando` mean?
cards.back: He or she fainted, fell, and is seizing. All three go straight to the nurse; for a fall, ask about blood thinners, and for a seizure, note the time it started.

cards.front: Which Spanish phrases signal the stroke pathway?
cards.back: `no siente el brazo` (cannot feel the arm), `no puede hablar` (cannot speak), `no puede mover` (cannot move). Next question: `¿Cuándo fue la última vez que estaba bien?`

cards.front: How do you relay an urgent Spanish statement to the nurse?
cards.back: Who, the patient's exact words, and how long ago. "Room 12, the daughter says `se desmayó` about ten minutes ago." Never substitute a diagnosis for the words.

cards.front: What do you do when you only half understood something urgent?
cards.back: Escalate it anyway, exactly as if you had understood it fully. Say `No entiendo, un momento`, then get the nurse and the interpreter. A half-caught alarm is still an alarm.

quiz.q: Under federal law, what must a hospital receiving federal funds provide to a patient with limited English proficiency?
choices: A qualified interpreter at no cost to the patient
A discount on the visit if no interpreter is available
Written materials only, in the patient's language
A bilingual staff member if one happens to be working
quiz.why: Title VI and ACA Section 1557 require free language assistance. Written material alone does not satisfy a spoken clinical encounter, a discount is irrelevant, and an untrained bilingual employee is an ad hoc interpreter, not a qualified one.

quiz.q: A 68-year-old Spanish-speaking woman is in your room for a possible appendicitis. Her 12-year-old granddaughter offers to interpret while you ask about her allergies. What is the correct action?
choices: Let the granddaughter interpret; allergies are a simple question
Decline, call the interpreter line, and keep the granddaughter as family only
Use the granddaughter now and re-confirm with an interpreter at discharge
Ask the patient to point to allergy names on a printed list
quiz.why: A child is never an acceptable interpreter outside a true seconds-count emergency, and allergies are charted clinical content that drives drug administration. Re-confirming later still means the first dose could be given on a child's translation.

quiz.q: You are on the interpreter phone getting a history. Which practice most reduces interpretation error?
choices: Speaking in long complete paragraphs so context is preserved
Addressing the interpreter directly with "ask her" phrasing
Speaking one idea per sentence, to the patient, and pausing
Having a side conversation with the nurse while the interpreter relays
quiz.why: Short single-idea segments prevent the summarizing that drops details. Long paragraphs force compression, ask-her phrasing sidelines the patient, and English side conversations exclude the patient from her own encounter.

quiz.q: A patient is in respiratory arrest. No interpreter is reachable and only the patient's adult son speaks both languages. What is the defensible course?
choices: Wait for the interpreter line; policy has no exceptions
Proceed with no communication at all until an interpreter connects
Have the son sign a consent form on the patient's behalf
Use the son to communicate now, get a qualified interpreter as soon as possible, and document the emergency and what was done
quiz.why: A true seconds-count emergency is the one recognized exception to the ad hoc interpreter rule, but it is time-limited and must be documented. Waiting harms the patient, silence is not an option, and a family member does not gain consent authority by being bilingual.

quiz.q: Which Spanish letter is always silent?
quiz.why: `h` is never pronounced, so `hospital` is os-pee-TAHL and `herida` is eh-REE-dah. `j` is a throaty English h, `ll` is a y sound, and `ñ` is ny.

quiz.q: How is `cirugía` pronounced?
quiz.why: The c before i is an s, the g before i is the throaty h, and the written accent puts the stress on the i. Hard g and j sounds are the two usual errors.

quiz.q: A patient is asked about pills and answers with the stress clearly on the final syllable: toh-MOH. What does the stress tell you?
choices: It is a question rather than a statement
It means I take them daily
It is past tense, he or she took them, which in this context suggests an ingestion
quiz.why: `tomó` with final stress is third-person past. `tomo` with second-to-last stress is I take, a home medication. In an overdose history the two mean opposite things, which is why stress is not optional.

quiz.q: Which is the correct respectful way to address a 79-year-old male patient?
choices: His first name alone, to keep things informal
`señorita`, which is a general courtesy title
quiz.why: `usted` with a title is the default for every adult and matters most with elders. `tú` reads as condescending, a bare first name skips an expected courtesy, and `señorita` applies to a young woman.

quiz.q: You are about to roll up a patient's sleeve for a blood pressure. Which sequence is correct?
choices: Roll the sleeve, then say `Con permiso`
Say `Voy a levantarle la manga. ¿Está bien?`, then roll the sleeve
Ask the family member's permission first
Say nothing; a blood pressure is routine
quiz.why: Announce with `Voy a...` and confirm with `¿Está bien?` before touching. Touching first makes the courtesy meaningless, the family is not the decision-maker for a competent adult, and silence is what reads as rude.

quiz.q: The wristband reads García Rivera, María Elena. The patient says `María Elena García Rivera`. What is the correct interpretation?
choices: The wristband belongs to a different patient
The patient is confused about her own name
The names match; Spanish names carry two surnames and registration systems reorder them
The second surname is a data-entry error and should be removed
quiz.why: Father's surname then mother's surname is standard, and registration commonly inverts or truncates them. Confirm with the date of birth rather than assuming a mismatch or editing a legal name out of the record.

quiz.q: What is the Spanish word for the number eleven?
quiz.why: `once` is eleven. `uno` is one, `diez` is ten, `doce` is twelve. Hearing `once` as the English word once is a documented source of missed overdoses.

quiz.q: A 45-year-old woman tells you her weight is `sesenta y cinco`. What do you chart?
choices: Nothing yet; ask `¿en libras o en kilos?` and chart the number with the unit she confirms
65 kilograms, since most patients use metric
quiz.why: The number is meaningless without the unit. Assuming either way risks a large weight-based dosing error, and converting from an assumption simply locks the error in. Ask, then chart what she confirmed.

quiz.q: A patient with a cough reports `tengo treinta y ocho y medio`. What should the nurse hear from you?
choices: A pain score of 38 and a half, which is not a valid scale
A reported fever of 38.5 C, roughly 101.3 F, which you should confirm with a measured temperature
quiz.why: Celsius is the everyday temperature scale outside the US, and 38.5 C is 101.3 F. Reporting it as a raw number invites misreading, so give the unit and then confirm it with your own measurement.

quiz.q: Which phrase correctly anchors a numeric pain scale in Spanish?
choices: `Cero es nada, diez es lo peor.`
quiz.why: Anchoring defines the endpoints of the scale. The other three ask about location, change over time, and duration, none of which tells the patient what zero and ten mean.

quiz.q: What does `la espalda` mean?
quiz.why: `la espalda` is the back. The shoulder is `el hombro`, the chest is `el pecho`, and the stomach is `el estómago` or `la barriga`.

quiz.q: A 58-year-old man with diaphoresis says `siento una opresión en el pecho`. What do you report to the nurse?
choices: His exact words, that he feels pressure in his chest, and that he is diaphoretic
That he has mild chest discomfort
quiz.why: `opresión` is the squeezing, heavy quality typical of ischemic pain, and with diaphoresis it is a 12-lead within 10 minutes. Softening it to discomfort or guessing a diagnosis removes the finding that drives the pathway.

quiz.q: Without an interpreter, what is the most reliable way to localize a patient's pain?
choices: Ask `¿Qué le pasa?` and listen carefully
Point to or hover over each region and ask `¿aquí?` while watching the face
Have the patient write the location down
Ask the family member where it hurts
