quiz.why: Pointing plus `¿aquí?` requires no grammar from either side and gives you a facial response you can trust. An open question needs interpretation, writing assumes literacy, and family report is secondhand.

quiz.q: A 70-year-old woman says she is `mareada` and also reports `falta de aire`. Which combination best reflects what you should hand off?
choices: She is dizzy from anxiety and needs reassurance
She has vertigo and needs to be kept still
She reports a vague dizziness plus shortness of breath, so a pulse oximetry reading and the nurse are needed before anyone interprets the dizziness
She is nauseated and should be offered water
quiz.why: `mareada` is ambiguous between lightheaded, spinning, and nauseated, so it should not be converted into a diagnosis. Shortness of breath is objective and measurable, so get the number first. Offering water ignores possible nothing-by-mouth status.

quiz.q: What does `¿Desde cuándo?` ask?
choices: Since when, meaning how long has this been going on
quiz.why: `¿Desde cuándo?` asks duration. Location is `¿Dónde le duele?`, severity is `¿Cuánto le duele?`, and allergies are `¿Tiene alergias?`

quiz.q: A 30-year-old man with nasal congestion and a cough says `estoy constipado`. What is charted correctly?
choices: Nasal congestion, consistent with an upper respiratory complaint
Constipation, with an abdominal exam indicated
Both congestion and constipation, to be safe
quiz.why: `constipado` means congested. Constipated is `estreñido`. Charting a bowel complaint here creates a false problem and can trigger imaging or interventions the patient never needed.

quiz.q: A patient with right arm weakness answers `hace tres horas, de repente`. What two facts have you just captured?
choices: Three hours of gradually worsening symptoms
quiz.why: `hace tres horas` is three hours ago and `de repente` is suddenly. Both matter: onset time governs stroke treatment windows, and sudden onset raises the suspicion of a vascular event over a gradual process.

quiz.q: A vomiting patient says `creo que estoy intoxicada`. What is the most accurate handoff?
choices: She reports feeling poisoned, most often meaning food poisoning, and the actual cause still needs an interpreted history
quiz.why: `intoxicado` means poisoned and is used most often for foodborne illness, not intoxication. Drunk is `borracho` or `ebrio`. Because the word is broad, the specific exposure has to come from an interpreted history, not from your guess.

quiz.q: What does `Acuéstese` mean?
quiz.why: `Acuéstese` is lie down. Sit down is `Siéntese`, turn over is `Dese vuelta`, and raise your arm is `Levante el brazo`.

quiz.q: You have flash in the hub of the needle and the tube is filling. What is the next thing to say?
quiz.why: Open the hand once you are in the vein; prolonged fist clenching can alter potassium results. The fist and the stick warning come before, and pressure on gauze comes after the needle is out.

quiz.q: Your 12-lead keeps showing muscle artifact on a nervous patient. Which phrase addresses the cause?
quiz.why: Talking and muscle tension are the main sources of baseline artifact, so quiet and relaxed fixes it. A deep breath moves the chest, a fist tenses the arm, and raising the arm guarantees artifact.

quiz.q: An older woman becomes visibly distressed when you approach with 12-lead electrodes. Best next step?
choices: Proceed quickly so it is over sooner
Skip the precordial leads and run a limb-lead-only tracing
Close the curtain, say `Voy a ponerle unos parches en el pecho. Es para ver el corazón. Son diez segundos.`, keep a sheet over what is not in use, and offer a female staff member
Wait for a family member to explain it to her
quiz.why: Explaining, covering, and offering a female staff member addresses modesty without delaying a time-sensitive study. Rushing escalates the distress, a partial tracing is diagnostically inadequate, and family are not interpreters.

quiz.q: What does `De adelante hacia atrás` instruct?
quiz.why: It is the direction of cleaning for a clean-catch urine specimen, which reduces periurethral contamination. The other options are positioning and pressure commands.

quiz.q: Twenty minutes after you apply a forearm splint, the patient says `no siento los dedos`. What does this mean and what do you do?
choices: She cannot feel her fingers; tell the nurse immediately, since a splint that has become too tight is a neurovascular emergency
She cannot move her fingers, which is expected in a splint
Her fingers are cold, which is normal after ice
She does not want the splint, so remove it and rewrap loosely
quiz.why: `no siento los dedos` is loss of sensation distal to the splint and suggests compression or swelling. New numbness is never expected, and a tech does not independently remove or rewrap a provider-applied splint; escalate it.

quiz.q: A patient with a forearm laceration asks in Spanish whether she will need stitches. What is the correct response?
choices: Say `Necesita puntos` if it looks deep
Say `El doctor le va a explicar` and get the provider with an interpreter
Say `No necesita puntos` to reassure her
quiz.why: Whether a wound needs repair is a provider decision and a clinical conversation, so it goes through the interpreter. Answering either way is practicing outside your scope, and a blanket reassurance promises an outcome you do not control.

quiz.q: A 72-year-old with new facial droop and slurred speech asks `¿me puede dar agua?`. What do you do?
choices: Give a small cup of water
Tell the nurse and hold all oral intake until a swallow screen is completed
Have the daughter decide whether it is safe
quiz.why: Stroke symptoms carry aspiration risk until a swallow screen is passed, and ice chips are still oral intake. The decision belongs to the nurse or provider, not to the tech and not to the family.

quiz.q: A family waits while a patient is being resuscitated. A relative asks you in Spanish whether he will be okay. Which reply is both honest and supportive?
choices: Tell them the patient is in cardiac arrest and the odds are poor
`Estamos cuidándole. El doctor va a venir a hablar con ustedes.`
quiz.why: It states what is true and names who will bring the news. A promise of a good outcome can be falsified within minutes, silence abandons them, and delivering the prognosis is outside a tech's scope.

quiz.q: You are walking past the waiting room when a woman grabs your arm and says something fast that includes `mi esposo` and `no puede respirar`. You caught only those words. What is the correct action?
choices: Go with her immediately, get eyes on the husband, call the nurse, and put a pulse oximeter on him
Ask her to wait while you find an interpreter
Direct her to the registration desk to be triaged in order
Ask another patient in the lobby to translate the full sentence
quiz.why: Partial understanding of an airway or breathing complaint is still an alarm, and the response is to look and get a number. Waiting for an interpreter or for registration burns time, and recruiting a bystander is an ad hoc interpreter and a privacy breach.

scenarios.title: Room 9: vitals and a 12-lead, no shared language
scenarios.intro:
It is 1450 on a Tuesday. The charge nurse hands you a printout: Room 9, 61-year-old man, walked in with chest discomfort, triaged five minutes ago. Under language it says Spanish. The note reads: patient speaks minimal English, daughter at bedside.

Your orders are a full set of vitals and a 12-lead ECG. The department is full and the nurse is in another room. You speak no Spanish beyond the phrases you have practiced.

steps.prompt:
You are at the door. The patient is sitting upright on the stretcher in street clothes, pale, with one hand resting flat on his sternum. A woman in her thirties stands next to him and looks up as you come in.

What is your opening move?

choices.text: Walk to the cart, start the blood pressure cuff, and get the numbers first since he looks uncomfortable
choices.feedback: Speed is right, but entering a room silently and going straight for an arm reads as rude and starts the encounter badly. A seven-second greeting costs you nothing and buys cooperation for the next twenty minutes.

choices.text: `Buenas tardes. Hola, me llamo Jose, soy técnico de emergencias.` Then `Voy a tomarle los signos vitales` and start the cuff while you press the interpreter call
choices.feedback: Correct. Greet, name, role, announce the task, and get the interpreter moving in parallel. Vitals and an ECG are task commands inside your lane; nothing here waits on the interpreter.

choices.text: Ask the daughter to interpret the whole encounter so it goes faster
choices.feedback: No. She is family, not a qualified interpreter, and the history that follows is clinical. She is also a useful source of baseline once an interpreter is on, but she is not the channel.

choices.text: Step out to find an interpreter tablet before doing anything in the room
choices.feedback: This delays a set of vitals on a pale man holding his chest. Vitals and a 12-lead do not require an interpreter, and the tablet can be dialed from inside the room while you work.

steps.prompt:
The cuff cycles. He is diaphoretic and his shirt collar is damp. His daughter says `desde la mañana, le duele el pecho`.

You have about four seconds to decide what that changed.

choices.text: Note that his chest has hurt since this morning, say `Ya viene el intérprete`, and immediately get the 12-lead on him while calling out to the nurse that this is chest pain since morning with diaphoresis
choices.feedback: Correct. `desde la mañana` is since this morning and `le duele el pecho` is his chest hurts. Chest pain plus diaphoresis is a 12-lead within 10 minutes of arrival, and the nurse needs to hear the words now.

choices.text: Finish the full vital set and temperature, then chart, then set up the ECG
choices.feedback: The temperature is already recorded and the ECG is the time-sensitive item. Sequencing the low-yield task ahead of the tracing burns minutes off a 10-minute clock.

choices.text: Ask the daughter in English for a full pain history before anything else
choices.feedback: History through a family member is both outside the interpreter rule and slower than the tracing. Get the ECG, then let the interpreted history happen around it.

steps.prompt:
You have the 12-lead machine at the bedside. He is in a button-down shirt. His daughter is standing at the head of the bed.

How do you get the electrodes on?

choices.text: Open his shirt without comment and place the leads; it is faster and he is having chest pain
choices.feedback: Speed matters, but an unannounced exposure on a patient who cannot ask what you are doing is frightening and sometimes ends in refusal, which costs more time than the sentence would have.

choices.text: Close the curtain, say `Voy a ponerle unos parches en el pecho. Es para ver el corazón. No duele. Son diez segundos.`, drape a sheet, then place the leads
choices.feedback: Correct. Four short sentences, all within your lane, all true. Curtain and drape handle modesty without adding a minute.

choices.text: Wait for the interpreter to connect so you can explain the ECG in full before placing anything
choices.feedback: A 12-lead is a non-invasive task you can announce yourself. Holding the tracing for an interpreter on a chest pain patient is exactly the delay the 10-minute standard exists to prevent.

choices.text: Ask the daughter to undress him while you get the machine ready
choices.feedback: This hands a clinical task to a family member and removes your own observation of the chest wall. Announce it and do it yourself.

steps.prompt:
The tracing prints with a wandering, fuzzy baseline in every lead. He is talking to his daughter and shifting on the stretcher.

What do you say?

choices.text: `No hable, relájese. No se mueva. Respire normal.` then repeat the tracing
choices.feedback: Correct. Talking and muscle tension are the two usual artifact sources, and these are the exact commands for both. Repeating a clean tracing takes ten seconds.

choices.text: Send the artifact-heavy tracing; the machine's interpretation will still be read by the physician
choices.feedback: An uninterpretable tracing is not a tracing. Artifact can hide or mimic ST changes, and the physician will simply order it again, which costs more than repeating it now.

choices.text: `Apriete el puño.` to steady the arm, then reprint
choices.feedback: That is a phlebotomy command and it tenses the arm, which makes artifact worse. The right instruction is to stop talking and stay still.

steps.prompt:
Clean tracing in hand at 1458, eight minutes after his arrival in the room. The interpreter video cart has connected and the nurse is walking in.

Last decision: what do you hand over?

choices.text: "Room 9, vitals are up, ECG done."
choices.feedback: Accurate but hollow. You are dropping the two findings that set the priority: the patient's own description and the onset time.

choices.text: "Room 9, 61-year-old, tracing is from 1458. Daughter says `desde la mañana, le duele el pecho`, chest pain since this morning. He is diaphoretic, 158 over 92, 96 percent on room air. Interpreter is connected on the cart."
choices.feedback: Correct. Who, the patient's own words, the timing, the objective findings, and the fact that a qualified interpreter is already up. That is a complete handoff with nothing invented.

choices.text: "Room 9 looks like an MI, get the cath lab on standby."
choices.feedback: You do not read the tracing or make the diagnosis, and calling it prematurely can bias the read. Give the findings and the timing and let the physician interpret them.

scenarios.debrief:
## The pattern

The interpreter rule and speed are not in conflict. Vitals, positioning, a 12-lead, and a blood draw are task commands you can announce yourself; the history, the consent, and the explanation wait for the interpreter, and the interpreter gets dialed in parallel rather than before you start.

Three things carried this case. `Voy a...` before every touch, so nothing was a surprise. Recognizing `le duele el pecho` and `desde la mañana` well enough to start the 10-minute ECG clock. And handing the nurse the patient's actual words instead of a diagnosis.

> **Key:** Announce, act, escalate in the patient's own words. When you report what was said rather than what you concluded, the clinician who does interpret it is working from the real data.

The artifact step is the one people underrate. A tracing full of movement noise is not a faster tracing, it is a repeat, and the two sentences that fix it take less time than reprinting.

scenarios.title: The hallway: a daughter says something urgent
scenarios.intro:
It is 2310 and you are pushing a stretcher of clean linen down the main corridor. The waiting room is full. A woman in her forties steps in front of you, points back toward the lobby, and says something quickly.

You catch three things: `mi papá`, `se cayó`, and `toma pastillas para la sangre`. You do not catch anything else. She is not shouting, but she is not waiting for you to finish what you are doing either.

steps.prompt:
You have a stretcher in your hands, a full lobby behind her, and three words.

What do you do first?

choices.text: Say `Un momento` and finish delivering the linen, then come back
choices.feedback: No. You have heard fall plus a blood medication in the same sentence, which is a head-bleed risk until proven otherwise. Linen waits.

choices.text: Park the stretcher against the wall, say `Ya voy`, and go with her to look at her father
choices.feedback: Correct. `mi papá` and `se cayó` are enough. Eyes on the patient is the first move for any reported fall, and `Ya voy` buys you the four seconds it takes to move the stretcher.

choices.text: Direct her to the registration desk so her father can be triaged properly
choices.feedback: He may well need registration, but you were told he fell and takes a blood medication. Sending her to a line without looking is how a lobby deterioration gets found late.

choices.text: Ask a bilingual patient in the lobby to translate the rest of what she said
choices.feedback: That is an ad hoc interpreter and a privacy breach in a public room. You already have enough words to act on.

steps.prompt:
Her father is in a lobby chair, awake, with an ice pack someone gave him held against the left side of his forehead. There is a small laceration above the eyebrow, oozing. He looks at you and says `estoy bien`.

His daughter says `se cayó en la escalera` and repeats `toma pastillas para la sangre`.

choices.text: Accept `estoy bien` and tell the daughter he will be called in turn
choices.feedback: `estoy bien` means I am fine, and it is what almost every older patient says. It is not a substitute for an assessment, and it does not cancel an anticoagulated head strike.

choices.text: Recognize that `toma pastillas para la sangre` means he takes blood medication, most likely an anticoagulant, and get the nurse now because this is a head injury on a blood thinner
choices.feedback: Correct. Anticoagulation plus head trauma is the combination that turns a minor fall into a CT and a bleed risk, even with a normal exam and a GCS of 15. The nurse needs it now, not at the next lobby round.

choices.text: Clean and dress the laceration first, since that is the visible injury
choices.feedback: The forehead cut is the least important thing in this picture. Treating the visible wound and deferring the head-injury escalation is exactly the inversion the phrase `pastillas para la sangre` should prevent.

steps.prompt:
The nurse is coming. She asks you two questions on the way: what does he take, and when did this happen.

You have a daughter who speaks Spanish, a patient who says `estoy bien`, and no interpreter yet.

choices.text: Guess warfarin, since that is the most common blood thinner in older patients
choices.feedback: Never guess a drug name. Warfarin, apixaban, rivaroxaban, and clopidogrel are managed very differently, and a guessed name in a handoff gets repeated as fact.

choices.text: Ask `¿Desde cuándo?` and `¿Tiene las pastillas?` to get the timing and the actual bottles, report exactly `toma pastillas para la sangre` without naming a drug, and get the interpreter up for the medication list
choices.feedback: Correct. Duration and the physical bottles are both things you can obtain yourself. The drug name is charted clinical content and belongs to an interpreted history.

choices.text: Have the daughter recite the full medication list in English for the chart
choices.feedback: The medication list drives reversal decisions and is exactly the clinical content that requires a qualified interpreter. Ask her to bring the bottles instead, which is an object, not a translation.

steps.prompt:
He is moved to a bed. The daughter hands you a bag with four pill bottles. The interpreter video cart is connecting. The patient is quiet, keeps his eyes closed, and rubs his forehead.

He says something you do not catch at all, twice.

choices.text: Nod and say `sí, sí` so he feels heard, then carry on
choices.feedback: Agreeing with something you did not understand is how a new complaint disappears. He is a head strike on an anticoagulant, and a repeated sentence is the last thing you want to nod past.

choices.text: Say `No entiendo, un momento` and `Ya viene el intérprete`, stay with him, and tell the nurse he is repeating something you could not understand
choices.feedback: Correct. Admitting you did not understand is a clinical action, not a failure. Flagging a repeated unintelligible complaint in an anticoagulated head injury is how a worsening headache gets caught.

choices.text: Ask the daughter to tell you what he said
choices.feedback: Understandable, and in a true emergency it would be defensible, but the interpreter is seconds away and a symptom report is clinical content. Hold it for the cart.

steps.prompt:
The interpreter connects. Through her, he says he has a bad headache and feels like vomiting, and it started about ten minutes ago in the chair. The nurse is at the computer two feet away.

What do you do with that?

choices.text: Tell the nurse out loud right now: new headache and nausea, onset about ten minutes ago, in an anticoagulated head strike
choices.feedback: Correct. New or worsening headache with vomiting after a head injury on an anticoagulant is the deterioration pattern that pushes imaging urgency. Saying it out loud beats charting it.

choices.text: Chart it in the nursing note so it is documented accurately
choices.feedback: Documenting is necessary but it is not communication. A note is read minutes to hours later; a sentence spoken to the nurse standing next to you is read now.

choices.text: Offer him water and a basin and see whether the nausea settles
choices.feedback: Water is wrong twice over: he may need urgent imaging and possibly the operating room, so he should be nothing by mouth, and waiting to see is exactly the wrong response to a new post-traumatic headache.

scenarios.debrief:
## The pattern

Three Spanish fragments carried this entire case: `se cayó`, `toma pastillas para la sangre`, and `no entiendo`. None of them required fluency. They required recognition and a willingness to stop what you were doing.

The clinical spine is a familiar one. A fall plus an anticoagulant plus a head strike is a CT question even when the patient is awake, oriented, and insisting `estoy bien`. A normal exam and a GCS of 15 do not exclude an intracranial bleed, and the classic story is exactly this: fine at first, then a new headache and vomiting.

> **Key:** Recognize, relay verbatim, and never fill a gap with a guess. `Toma pastillas para la sangre` goes to the nurse as those words plus the actual bottles, not as a drug name you assumed.

> **Trap:** `estoy bien` and a nod are the two easiest ways to lose a deterioration. Saying `No entiendo, un momento` out loud is faster, safer, and more professional than pretending.
